column1: What is generalization error in classification?
column2: It is the expected error of a classification model over random records selected from the underlying data distribution.

column1: How do training error and test error differ?
column2: Training error is calculated on the training dataset, whereas test error is calculated on a separate, unseen test dataset.

column1: What defines model underfitting in classification?
column2: Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple, resulting in high errors on both the training set and the test set.

column1: What defines model overfitting in classification?
column2: Overfitting occurs when a model is overly complex, yielding a small training error but a high test error.

column1: How does increasing the training sample size affect model overfitting?
column2: Increasing training data size reduces the difference between training error and test error for a given model complexity.

column1: What is the primary purpose of a validation set during model building?
column2: A validation set is used to estimate generalization error and tune model complexity without exposing the test set.

column1: How does Occam's Razor apply to classification model selection?
column2: Given models with similar generalization error, Occam's Razor dictates choosing the simpler model over the more complex one.

column1: What is the formula for classification accuracy using confusion matrix terms?
column2: $\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{\text{TP} + \text{TN} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}}$

column1: Why is standard accuracy a misleading performance metric for heavily imbalanced datasets?
column2: A trivial model predicting only the majority class achieves high accuracy while failing to detect any rare class instances.

column1: How does $k$-fold cross-validation partition and evaluate data?
column2: It divides data into $k$ disjoint subsets, iteratively training on $k-1$ folds and testing on the remaining fold.

column1: How does stratified cross-validation differ from standard $k$-fold cross-validation?
column2: Stratified cross-validation guarantees that each fold maintains the same class label proportions as the original dataset.

column1: What defines leave-one-out cross-validation?
column2: It is an extreme form of $k$-fold cross-validation where $k$ equals the total sample size $n$, testing on one instance at a time.

column1: Which performance metrics form the axes of an ROC curve?
column2: The y-axis represents the True Positive Rate (TPR) and the x-axis represents the False Positive Rate (FPR).

column1: What is the formula for True Positive Rate (TPR)?
column2: $\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}$

column1: What is the formula for False Positive Rate (FPR)?
column2: $\text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}$

column1: In an ROC plot formatted as $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$, what does the coordinate $(0,0)$ represent?
column2: It represents a classifier that predicts every record to belong to the negative class.

column1: In an ROC plot formatted as $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$, what does the coordinate $(1,1)$ represent?
column2: It represents a classifier that predicts every record to belong to the positive class.

column1: In an ROC plot formatted as $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$, what does the coordinate $(1,0)$ represent?
column2: It represents an ideal classifier with perfect true positive detection and zero false positives.

column1: What performance level is indicated by the diagonal line in an ROC curve?
column2: The diagonal line represents the expected performance of random guessing.

column1: How is the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) interpreted for model quality?
column2: An ideal classifier has an AUC of $1.0$, whereas random guessing yields an AUC of $0.5$.

column1: How are continuous classifier outputs used to construct a discrete step ROC curve?
column2: Test records are sorted by score in decreasing order, and unique scores serve as thresholds to compute $(\text{TPR}, \text{FPR})$ points.

column1: What defines a class imbalance problem in data mining?
column2: It occurs when records from one majority class heavily outnumber instances of a rare target class.

column1: What is the cost matrix notation $C(i|j)$?
column2: $C(i|j)$ denotes the cost associated with misclassifying an instance of actual class $j$ as predicted class $i$.

column1: In cost-sensitive classification, under what condition is a test record classified as positive?
column2: A record is classified as positive when the expected cost of predicting positive is strictly less than predicting negative ($\ meast{Cost}(+) < \text{Cost}(-)$).

column1: How do under-sampling and over-sampling techniques differ in handling class imbalance?
column2: Under-sampling removes instances from the majority class, whereas over-sampling replicates or adds instances to the rare class.

column1: Which confusion matrix outcomes bias the Precision metric?
column2: Precision is biased towards True Positives ($C(\text{Yes}|\text{Yes})$) and False Positives ($C(\text{Yes}|\text{No})$).

column1: Which confusion matrix outcomes bias the Recall metric?
column2: Recall is biased towards True Positives ($C(\text{Yes}|\text{Yes})$) and False Negatives ($C(\text{No}|\text{Yes})$).

column1: In hypothesis testing terms applied to confusion matrices, what corresponds to a Type I error ($\alpha$)?
column2: A Type I error ($\alpha$) corresponds to a False Positive ($\text{FP}$), which is rejecting a true null hypothesis.

column1: In hypothesis testing terms applied to confusion matrices, what corresponds to a Type II error ($\beta$)?
column2: A Type II error ($\beta$) corresponds to a False Negative ($\text{FN}$), which is accepting a false null hypothesis.

column1: What is the strategy of class-based ordering for handling imbalanced class rules?
column2: It assigns higher priority to classification rules that predict the rare class.

column1: What is another name for training errors?
column2: Apparent errors: the errors committed on the training set.

column1: Why can't training error be used to estimate generalization error?
column2: It does not reflect how well the model performs on previously unseen records, especially when the model overfits.

column1: What three approaches are listed for estimating generalization error during model selection?
column2: Using a validation set, incorporating model complexity, and estimating statistical bounds.

column1: What is the drawback of using a validation set for model selection?
column2: Less data is available for training.

column1: Besides the learning algorithm, what factors can a model's measured performance depend on?
column2: The class distribution, the cost of misclassification, and the size of the training and test sets.

column1: What extra information does repeated cross-validation provide?
column2: An estimate of the variance of the generalization error.

column1: When is stratified cross-validation especially important?
column2: When classes are imbalanced and the sample is small.

column1: What must a classifier produce in order to draw an ROC curve?
column2: Continuous-valued outputs (scores) that can rank test records from most to least likely positive.

column1: What trade-off does an ROC curve display?
column2: Detection rate (TPR) against false alarm rate (FPR) as the classifier's threshold changes.

column1: What is the formula for Precision?
column2: $p = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}$

column1: Recall is the same quantity as which rate plotted on an ROC curve?
column2: The True Positive Rate (TPR): $r = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$.

column1: What is the formula for the F-measure?
column2: $F = \frac{2rp}{r + p} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}$

column1: Which confusion matrix cell is the F-measure NOT biased towards?
column2: $C(\text{No}|\text{No})$, the true negatives; it depends on all other cells.

column1: What implicit cost assumption does the standard Bayes rule (predict + if $p(+|x) > p(-|x)$) make?
column2: That $C(+|+) = C(-|-) = 0$ and $C(+|-) = C(-|+)$: correct predictions are free and both errors cost the same.

column1: With zero cost for correct predictions, what is the cost-sensitive threshold for predicting +?
column2: Predict + if $p(+|x) > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}}$, where $C_{FP}$ and $C_{FN}$ are the costs of a false positive and a false negative.

column1: What does it mean when two ROC curves cross?
column2: Neither model consistently outperforms the other: one is better at small FPR, the other at large FPR.
